scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Chang dance originates from the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, specifically within the districts of Sikar, Churu, Jhunjhunu, and Bikaner.
It is a traditional folk form that has historically been performed in the border districts of the state.
The dance is seasonal, tied to the Hindu calendar, beginning on the festival of Maha Shivaratri and concluding on Dhulandi, the day after Holi.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Chang dance is performed to celebrate the festival of Holi and the symbolic defeat of evil.
It is a time of communal joy following the completion of agricultural tasks.
The period of performance—from Maha Shivaratri to Dhulandi—marks a significant transition in the seasonal and religious calendar of Rajasthan.
Today it is a living tradition.

narration: The dance is a group performance where men move, sing, and carouse to the beat of the chang.
It is often performed in a village square known as a Chauk.
While the specific technical footwork is not detailed in the sources, it is described as a systematic and disciplined performance in its core regions.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The central instrument is the Chang (or duff), a large wooden tambourine-like drum with a radius of 2 to 3 feet, covered in sheepskin leather and decorated with turmeric and paintings.
Other essential instruments include bronze or iron cymbals and a bamboo flute with eight holes.
Listen for the Chang (duff), Cymbals (bronze or iron), Bamboo flute (8 holes), Ghungroo (anklets).

The sound is dominated by the deep, resonant thrum of the large sheepskin chang drum, punctuated by the sharp metallic clashing of bronze cymbals and the melodic trills of a seven-holed bamboo flute. The dancers' anklets provide a constant rhythmic jingle that matches the vocal energy of the Dhamaal songs.

scenes.title: The people

The dance is found throughout Rajasthan but is most 'disciplined' and 'systematic' in the Shekhawati region (Sikar, Churu, Jhunjhunu, and Bikaner).
